title: Marie Curie: A Life of Discovery
summary: The life of Marie Curie, who overcame barriers to study science, discovered polonium and radium, and became the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.
poll: Being determined is more important than being talented.

versions.title: Marie Curie Finds New Things
versions.text:
Marie Curie was a great scientist. She was born in Poland in 1867. As a girl, she loved to read. She loved to learn.

Back then, girls in Poland could not go to a university. So she saved up. She went to France. She went to a big school there. She was at the top of her class.

There she met a man named Pierre. He loved science, too. They wed. They did their work side by side.

She looked at rocks that gave off rays. The rays could not be seen. Then the two found two new elements. An element is a kind of stuff. All things are made of it. One was named for her home land. One was radium. It could glow in the dark!

In 1903, the two won a big prize. It is the Nobel Prize. She was the first woman to win it.

Then Pierre died. She kept on. In 1911, she won it once more. No one had won two.

The rays made her sick. She died in 1934. But we still use what she found. Her life shows that hard work pays off.

versions.title: Marie Curie: A Life of Discovery
versions.text:
Marie Curie was one of the greatest scientists of all time. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867. As a girl, she loved books and was very good at math and science.

At that time, women in Poland could not study at a university. But Marie did not give up. She worked as a teacher and saved her money for years. Then she moved to Paris, France, and studied at a famous university there. She finished at the top of her class.

In Paris, Marie met Pierre Curie, who was also a scientist. They got married and began to work together in a small, cold lab.

Marie studied rocks that gave off rays that no one could see. She and Pierre found two new elements. An element is a basic kind of stuff that can't be split into simpler stuff. They named the first one polonium, after Poland. They named the second one radium. It could glow in the dark!

In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize, a famous prize for science. Marie was the first woman ever to win it.

Sadly, Pierre died in a street accident in 1906. Marie kept working, and she became the first woman to teach at her university. In 1911, she won a second Nobel Prize. No one had ever won two before.

The rays she worked with were harmful, and they made her sick. She died in 1934. Today, her work still helps doctors and scientists. Her life shows that hard work can lead to great things.

In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with a third scientist. Marie was the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize.

Later, Marie helped doctors by putting X-ray machines in trucks. The trucks helped them find broken bones in hurt soldiers.

The rays she worked with were harmful, and they made her sick. She died in 1934. Today, her work still helps doctors and scientists all over the world.

versions.title: Marie Curie: A Life of Discovery

Marie Curie was one of the most important scientists in history. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867, and as a girl she loved books and was excellent at mathematics and science.

At that time, women in Poland were not allowed to study at a university. Marie was determined to learn anyway, so she worked as a teacher and saved her money for several years. Then she moved to Paris, France, where she studied physics and mathematics at a famous university. She finished at the top of her class.

In Paris, Marie met Pierre Curie, another talented scientist. They married and began working together in a small, chilly laboratory.

Marie investigated a metal called uranium, which gave off invisible rays. She named this energy radioactivity. Working with Pierre, she then discovered two new elements. They named the first one polonium, after Poland, and the second one radium, which could glow faintly in the dark.

In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with another scientist, Henri Becquerel. Marie became the first woman ever to receive a Nobel Prize.

Tragically, Pierre died in a street accident in 1906. Marie continued their research, and she became the first woman to teach at her university. In 1911, she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry. She was the first person ever to receive two.

During a war a few years later, Marie helped doctors by equipping trucks with X-ray machines. These mobile units allowed doctors to locate broken bones and other injuries in wounded soldiers.

The rays she studied were harmful, and years of exposure made her seriously ill. She died in 1934. Today, her discoveries continue to help doctors and scientists around the world.

versions.title: Marie Curie: A Pioneer of Discovery
versions.text:
Marie Curie was one of the most influential scientists in history, a pioneer whose work transformed both physics and medicine. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867, and as a girl she loved books and excelled at mathematics and science.

At that time, women in Poland were not permitted to study at a university. Marie was determined to continue learning, so she worked as a teacher and saved her earnings for several years. Eventually she moved to Paris, France, where she studied physics and mathematics at a famous university, finishing at the top of her class.

In Paris, Marie met Pierre Curie, another talented scientist, and they married and began working together in a small, chilly laboratory with very little equipment.

Marie investigated a metal called uranium, which emitted invisible radiation, a property she named radioactivity. Working with Pierre, she processed tons of rock and discovered two new elements. They named the first one polonium, after her homeland, and the second one radium, which could glow faintly in the dark.

In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with another scientist, Henri Becquerel. Marie became the first woman ever to receive a Nobel Prize, an achievement that brought her international recognition.

Tragically, Pierre died in a street accident in 1906. Marie continued their research alone, and she became the first woman to teach at her university. In 1911, she received a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry, and she remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

During a war a few years later, Marie assisted doctors by equipping trucks with X-ray machines. These mobile units allowed doctors to locate broken bones and other injuries in wounded soldiers.

Unfortunately, scientists did not yet understand the hazard that radiation posed to the human body. Years of exposure made Marie seriously ill, and she died in 1934. Even today, her notebooks are so radioactive that they are stored in protective boxes.

Her legacy endures in hospitals and laboratories throughout the world. Her daughter Irene also won a Nobel Prize, and Marie's persistence continues to inspire young scientists everywhere.

Marie Curie was one of the most influential scientists in history, a pioneer whose work transformed both physics and medicine. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867, and as a girl she was an enthusiastic reader who excelled at mathematics and science.

At that time, women in Poland were not permitted to study at a university, but Marie was determined to continue learning, so she worked as a teacher and saved her earnings for several years. Eventually she relocated to Paris, France, where she studied physics and mathematics at a prestigious university, graduating at the top of her class even though French was not her first language.

In Paris, Marie met Pierre Curie, another talented scientist, and they married and began working together in a small, chilly laboratory with remarkably little equipment.

Marie investigated a metal called uranium, which emitted invisible radiation, a property she named radioactivity. Collaborating with Pierre, she processed tons of mineral ore and ultimately discovered two previously unknown elements. They named the first one polonium, after her homeland, and the second one radium, which could glow faintly in the dark.

In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with another scientist, Henri Becquerel. Marie became the first woman ever to receive a Nobel Prize, an achievement that brought her international recognition.

Tragically, Pierre died in a street accident in 1906. Marie continued their research independently, and she became the first woman to teach at her university. In 1911, she received a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry, and she remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

During a war a few years later, Marie assisted physicians by equipping vehicles with X-ray machines, and these mobile units allowed doctors to locate broken bones and other injuries in wounded soldiers.

Unfortunately, scientists of that era did not yet understand the hazard that radiation posed to the human body. Years of exposure made Marie seriously ill, and she died in 1934. Even today, her notebooks are so radioactive that they are stored in protective boxes.

Her legacy endures in hospitals and laboratories throughout the world, since her research contributed to medical treatments that use radiation. Her daughter Irene also won a Nobel Prize, and Marie's persistence continues to inspire young scientists everywhere.

versions.title: Marie Curie: A Pioneer of Discovery
versions.text:
Marie Curie was one of the most influential scientists in recorded history, a pioneer whose extraordinary investigations transformed both physics and medicine. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867, and as a girl she was an enthusiastic reader who excelled at mathematics and science.

At that time, women in Poland were not permitted to study at a university, but Marie was determined to continue learning, so she worked as a private tutor and accumulated her modest earnings for several years. Eventually she relocated to Paris, France, where she studied physics and mathematics at a prestigious university, graduating at the top of her class even though French was not her first language.

In Paris, Marie met Pierre Curie, another talented scientist, and they married and began working together in a small, chilly laboratory with remarkably little equipment.

Marie investigated a metal called uranium, which emitted invisible radiation, a property she named radioactivity. Collaborating with Pierre, she processed tons of mineral ore and ultimately discovered two previously unknown elements. They named the first one polonium, after her homeland, and the second one radium, which could glow faintly in the dark.

In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with another scientist, Henri Becquerel. Marie became the first woman ever to receive a Nobel Prize, an accomplishment that brought her immediate international recognition.

Tragically, Pierre died in a street accident in 1906, yet Marie continued their research independently, and she became the first woman to teach at her university. In 1911, she received a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry, and she remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

During a war a few years later, Marie assisted physicians by equipping vehicles with X-ray machines, and these mobile units enabled medical teams to identify fractured bones and other injuries in wounded soldiers.

Unfortunately, scientists of that era did not yet understand the hazard that radiation posed to the human body. Decades of continuous exposure made Marie seriously ill, and she died in 1934. Even today, her notebooks are so radioactive that they are preserved in protective, lead-lined boxes.

Her legacy endures in hospitals and laboratories throughout the world, since her research contributed to medical treatments that use radiation. Her daughter Irene also won a Nobel Prize, and Marie's extraordinary persistence continues to inspire aspiring scientists everywhere.

versions.title: Marie Curie: A Pioneer of Discovery
versions.text:
Marie Curie was one of the most influential scientists in recorded history, a pioneer whose extraordinary investigations transformed both physics and medicine. She was born in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867, and as a girl she was an enthusiastic reader who excelled at mathematics and science.

At that time, women in Poland were not permitted to study at a university, but Marie was determined to continue learning, so she worked as a private tutor and accumulated her modest earnings for several years. Eventually she relocated to Paris, France, where she studied physics and mathematics at a prestigious university, graduating at the top of her class even though French was not her first language.

In Paris, Marie met Pierre Curie, another exceptionally talented scientist, and they married and began collaborating in a small, poorly heated laboratory with remarkably little specialized equipment.

Marie systematically investigated a metallic element called uranium, which emitted invisible radiation, a property she named radioactivity. Collaborating with Pierre, she processed tons of mineral ore and ultimately discovered two previously unknown elements. They named the first one polonium, after her homeland, and the second one radium, which could glow faintly in the dark.

In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with another scientist, Henri Becquerel. Consequently, Marie became the first woman ever to receive a Nobel Prize, an accomplishment that brought her immediate international recognition.

Tragically, Pierre died in a street accident in 1906, yet Marie continued their research independently, and she became the first woman appointed to teach at her distinguished university. In 1911, she received a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry, and she remains the only individual to win Nobel Prizes in two different scientific disciplines.

During a war a few years later, Marie assisted physicians by equipping vehicles with X-ray machines, and these mobile units enabled medical teams to identify fractured bones and other injuries in wounded soldiers.

Unfortunately, scientists of that era did not yet comprehend the serious hazard that radiation posed to the human body, so they frequently handled radioactive materials without adequate protection. Decades of continuous exposure made Marie seriously ill, and she died in 1934. Even today, her notebooks are so radioactive that they are preserved in protective, lead-lined boxes.

Her legacy endures in hospitals and laboratories throughout the world, since her pioneering research contributed significantly to medical treatments that utilize radiation. Her daughter Irene also won a Nobel Prize, and Marie's extraordinary persistence continues to inspire aspiring scientists everywhere.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why Marie Curie is called a pioneer. Use at least three pieces of evidence from the article, and discuss both the benefits and the dangers of her work.
checklist: I explained what makes Marie Curie a pioneer, with at least three pieces of evidence.
I discussed both the benefits of her work and the hazard of radiation.
I organized my answer in clear paragraphs with transitions such as furthermore and however.
HIGH.modelAnswer:
Marie Curie is rightly called a pioneer because she broke boundaries that had kept women out of science for generations. She studied at a university in Paris after years of saving money as a teacher, finished at the top of her class, and went on to discover two new elements, polonium and radium. In 1903 she became the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize, and in 1911 she became the first person in history to win two, an achievement that brought her enormous recognition.

Furthermore, her work on radiation produced real benefits for other people, since doctors used her X-ray trucks to find broken bones in wounded soldiers. However, her discoveries also carried a serious hazard, because the very rays she studied eventually made her sick and led to her death in 1934. Even with that danger, her scientific legacy still helps doctors and scientists around the world today, which is exactly why she remains a pioneer whose impact outlived her.
